name: The example
why: ([0, 2, 5, 4, 6, 6], [1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2]). Two routes reach 2 for 5 minutes: 0 → 2 and 0 → 1 → 2. Both go on to 3 (5 − 1 = 4), to 4 and to 5, so those have 2 cheapest routes too. 0 → 1 → 3 costs 6, more than 4, so it is not counted.

name: Refunds
why: ([0, 1, 3, 2], [1, 1, 1, 1]). Negative times are fine in a DAG; Dijkstra's method gets 1 and 3 wrong here.

name: Stations before the start
why: ([0, 1, 2, None, None], [1, 1, 1, 0, 0]). 3 and 4 come before 0 in the order, and no route from 0 reaches them.

name: Ties count together
why: ([0, 1, 1, 2], [1, 1, 1, 2]). The direct line costs 3, more than 2, so it is not counted.

name: A cheaper way replaces the count
why: ([0, 5, 1, 2], [1, 1, 1, 1]). When a cheaper way is found, the count starts again from that way's count; it does not add to the old one.

name: A line given twice
why: ([0, 4], [1, 2]): two different lines, so two routes.

name: 40 layers of two
args: (80, [(0, 1, 0)] + [(2 * i + a, 2 * i + 2 + b, 1) for i in range(39) for a in range(2) for b in range(2)], 0)
expr: (lambda r: [len(r[0]), r[0].count(None), sum(x for x in r[0] if x is not None) % 1000000007, sum(r[1]) % 1000000007, r[0][-3:], r[1][-3:]])(dag_routes(args[0], list(args[1]), args[2]))
show: 40 layers of 2 stations, each joined to both stations of the next layer by lines of 1 minute
why: The last stations have 2³⁹ cheapest routes each, shown modulo 1,000,000,007. Listing routes one by one never ends.

name: A chain of 100,000, listed backwards
expr: (lambda r: [len(r[0]), r[0].count(None), sum(x for x in r[0] if x is not None) % 1000000007, sum(r[1]) % 1000000007, r[0][-3:], r[1][-3:]])(dag_routes(args[0], list(args[1]), args[2]))
show: 99999 → 99998 → … → 0 with times from −5 to 5, the lines listed from the far end (1 → 0 first)
why: Recursion goes 100,000 calls deep and fails. Rounds over all lines until nothing changes (Bellman–Ford) need 100,000 rounds here. Put the stations in topological order once (GRPH-5) and go through them in that order.

name: 100,000 stations, 250,000 lines
expr: (lambda r: [len(r[0]), r[0].count(None), sum(x for x in r[0] if x is not None) % 1000000007, sum(r[1]) % 1000000007, r[0][-3:], r[1][-3:]])(dag_routes(args[0], list(args[1]), args[2]))
show: 100,000 stations; every line goes forward in a hidden order; times from −3 to 3, plus a line of 3 minutes from each station to the next in that order
why: Many ties, so many counts above 1. O(V + E) with Kahn's method.
